description_ru: Диалог на собеседовании: кандидатка рассказывает о своём опыте, ошибках и о том, как справляется с трудными ситуациями.
text:
Helen: Good morning, Ms Okoro, and thank you for coming in. I am Helen Bryce, the director of Greenfield Trust, and this is my colleague Samir, who manages our volunteer programme.
Nadia: Good morning. Please call me Nadia. It is a pleasure to meet you both.
Samir: We have read your application with great interest. It says here that you have spent the last six years working for a city council. What made you decide to leave a secure job?
Nadia: That is a fair question. To be honest, I had been feeling for some time that I was sitting behind a desk while the real work was being done by other people. I was told by my manager last spring that I was too practical to be a bureaucrat, and I decided to take that as a compliment.

Helen: Let us talk about a project you are proud of. Could you describe one in detail?
Nadia: Certainly. Two years ago, I was asked to organise the cleaning of a river that runs through the eastern part of the city. The budget was tiny, so I contacted local schools, and about four hundred children took part. Altogether, nearly three tonnes of rubbish were collected in a single weekend.
Samir: That is impressive. Did everything go according to plan?
Nadia: Not at all. On the first morning, the delivery of gloves was delayed, and it started to pour with rain. I remember thinking that the whole event was going to fall flat. Then a teacher suggested we should use the waiting time to make tea for the parents, and that completely changed the mood.

Helen: How did you handle the pressure?
Nadia: I try to remember that most problems look worse in the first ten minutes than they really are. A former colleague once told me that panic is only a way of paying interest on a loan you have not borrowed. Since then I always take a short walk before I react.
Samir: That is a useful habit. And what about working in a team? Our staff are often described as strong-willed, and sometimes they disagree quite loudly.
Nadia: I am used to that. At the council, I was often the person who was asked to calm things down. I believe that people usually argue because they feel they are not being heard, so I try to listen first and talk second.

Helen: Let me ask you about a weakness. Everybody has one, so please do not tell me that you work too hard.
Nadia: Then I will be honest. I find it difficult to say no. Last year I took on three projects at once because I did not want to disappoint anyone, and one of them was completed late. My director said that she was not angry, but that it had cost the team some trust.
Samir: What did you learn from that experience?
Nadia: I learned to ask what can be postponed before I agree to anything new. Now I keep a list on my wall, and when it is full, I say that the next thing has to wait. It sounds simple, but it has saved me a great deal of stress.

Helen: Our work involves a lot of fundraising. Have you ever asked strangers for money?
Nadia: Only once, and it was not a success. I stood outside a supermarket for three hours with a bucket, and a man told me that he would give me five pounds if I could make him laugh. I told him a joke about a goldfish. He gave me two pounds and said that he had been laughing at me, not with me.
Samir: Well, two pounds is better than nothing.
Nadia: That is exactly what I said. In the end, I realised that people give more when they are told a true story, rather than when they are shown a statistic. After that, my bucket was never empty.

Helen: Let me explain something about the position. The coordinator will be responsible for sixty volunteers, and about half of them are teenagers. Some of them are only here because they were told to be by their schools.
Nadia: I find that quite encouraging, actually. In my experience, the reluctant ones often turn out to be the most loyal, as long as they are given real responsibility rather than boring jobs. When I was fifteen, I was forced to join a gardening club, and I have been grateful ever since.
Samir: Would you be comfortable working at weekends? The busiest periods are usually Saturdays and Sundays.
Nadia: Of course. I have no children, and my cat is quite independent. I would simply ask to take a day off during the week, if that is possible.

Helen: That is a good answer. Do you have any questions for us?
Nadia: Yes, two. First, how is success measured here, and who decides it? Second, what is the biggest problem the trust is facing at the moment?
Samir: Those are very good questions. Success is measured by the number of projects completed, but also by the number of volunteers who return. As for the biggest problem, we have been struggling to find enough money to keep our two part-time employees.
Nadia: Then I would like to help with that. I think I can bring both energy and a little humour, even if it only earns me two pounds at a time.

Helen: Thank you, Nadia. We will be making our decision by the end of next week, and you will be contacted by email.
Nadia: Thank you very much. Whatever the result is, I have really enjoyed this conversation.
Samir: So have we. By the way, you mentioned a goldfish joke. Would you mind telling it to us before you go?
Nadia: Only if you promise to laugh with me, and not at me.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Короткий звук, близкий к русскому ударному «а»; рот открыт нешироко.
Кончик языка не касается нёба; губы слегка вытянуты, звук без вибрации.
Плавное скольжение от «э» к «и»; не сокращайте до короткого «э».
Определите ударный слог (volunteer: -teer; application: -ca-) и произнесите его громче и длиннее.

questions.question: Where had Nadia worked for the last six years?
What project was she proud of?
questions.answer: Organising a river clean-up with about four hundred schoolchildren.

questions.question: What weakness did Nadia admit?
questions.answer: She finds it hard to say no and takes on too much.

questions.question: What is the trust's biggest problem?
questions.answer: Finding enough money to keep its two part-time employees.
